title: What the Ear Knows: What An Equalizer Can Teach Us About Reading and Writing
author: Terry Underwood
source: Learning to Read, Reading to Learn (terryu.substack.com), September 25, 2026
summary: Terry Underwood uses the craft of audio equalization as an extended analogy for teaching writing, revision and reading comprehension. He starts from the recording engineer's maxim "cut to fix, boost to flavor" and argues that most student drafts, like a muddy guitar track, already contain a worthwhile idea buried under hedges, throat-clearing and restated prompts, so revision is better understood as uncovering than adding. He borrows the engineer's sweep technique, exaggerating a habit until it becomes audible, as a classroom experiment for making invisible prose tics noticeable without turning them into rules. The high-pass filter and the Fletcher-Munson curves become lessons about cutting low-level deadwood and writing so that the structure survives a distracted, low-volume reading. In the final move Underwood turns the analogy toward the reader, picturing comprehension as a mix in which prior knowledge, purpose and expectation compete with the text. He warns that some readers let schema drown the text while others simply lack the knowledge and vocabulary to hear it, and that no fader can supply what the microphone never captured. Reading instruction, he concludes, must build knowledge and vocabulary rather than only balance resources students already have.
points: Underwood reframes revision as removal rather than addition: most drafts already hold the idea but bury it under hedges, restatements and throat-clearing he calls lard.
He adapts the engineer's narrow-band sweep into a classroom exercise in which students deliberately exaggerate hedges or abstract nouns to make habitual tics audible before deciding what to keep.
Writing should survive a distracted, low-volume reading, so concrete nouns, working verbs and paragraph-to-paragraph movement must carry the structure on their own.
Comprehension is pictured as a reader's mix in which prior knowledge can either drown out the text (the schema imposer) or be missing entirely.
Because no equalizer can raise a sound the microphone never captured, reading instruction must actively build background knowledge and vocabulary.
quotes: I have come to think that learning to EQ audio tracks has a great deal to teach us about reading and writing. Not because a sentence behaves like a sound wave, but because both kinds of work ask us to notice what is getting in the way.

Engineers have a maxim: cut to fix, boost to flavor. When something sounds wrong, the temptation is to add something, more treble for clarity or more bass for warmth. The better question runs the other way: what is obscuring the good sound?
But when something worth saying is already struggling to be heard, the draft needs what the Martin needs. Revision, at its best, is less an act of making than of revealing.

Teachers often tell students to “listen to your writing.” The engineer’s lesson is that sometimes you have to distort a thing before you can hear what you are doing to it. Then you restore it and decide.

Writers need to ask whether such material costs the reader more than it returns. That is not the same as asking whether everything can be shortened. An example earns its space by making a difficult idea accessible.
Make sure the essential structure is discernible to someone who won’t catch everything you intended. A piece of writing should survive being read partially, or badly.

The analogy helps me think about a reader whose prior knowledge booms so loudly that it drowns out the text: the schema imposer. They come away having read what they expected rather than what was written.

So teaching reading cannot be reduced to helping readers balance resources already at hand. For many students, the first job is to activate the knowledge they have that is relevant and then to search outside the text for new knowledge.
